11.0.s.en: 1. The crowning of David, the man of God, as king

11.0.0.en: 1 Then all Israel gathered themselves to David unto Hebron, saying, “Behold, we are thy bone and thy flesh. 2 And moreover in time past, even when Saul was king, thou wast he that leddest out and broughtest in Israel: and the LORD thy God said unto thee, Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be ruler over my people Israel.” 3 Therefore came all the elders of Israel to the king to Hebron; and David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the LORD; and they anointed David king over Israel, according to the word of the LORD by Samuel.

11.0.1.en: What is recorded in this chapter is taken from Second Samuel. What is said in [1-9] reflects what is recorded in (2 Sam 5:1-10); and [10-47] what is recorded in (2 Sam 23:8-39). The writer ignored everything recorded in the first four chapters of Second Samuel. He did not refer to the short reign of Ish-bosheth, nor to the troubles of Abner, nor to Joab’s stretching out his hand to kill Abner. Rather the writer went directly to the gathering of the tribes together at Hebron, David’s first capital before his capture of Jerusalem, in order to make him king. Here he brought out all Israel in a single unity.

11.0.2.en: The Second Book of Samuel presents to us in some detail how David the prophet reached the royal throne, whereas the Book of Chronicles is content to affirm that it was God who brought David to the throne, using many people, even some from the tribe of Benjamin, the brethren of Saul.

11.0.3.en: God is the Controller of history; He turns all things to the building up of His people, without compelling anyone to move by force.

11.0.4.en: Truly it seemed that many tried to hinder the work of God and His plan for His believers, but God turns even evil into good, as happened with Joseph the son of Jacob: his brothers intended evil against him, and the Lord wrought good for him through their evil.

11.0.5.en: Then all Israel gathered themselves to David unto Hebron, saying,

11.0.6.en: “Behold, we are thy bone and thy flesh. [1]

11.0.7.en: This book does not refer to the installation of David as king over Judah in Hebron; rather it begins with the gathering of all the tribes and their making him king over all.

11.0.8.en: The Book of Samuel recorded this period of history, and mentioned that David reigned for seven and a half years over the south, that is Judah, and that his capital was Hebron. This is not mentioned in Chronicles, because God looks upon Israel as one nation made up of twelve tribes; so from the standpoint of divine inspiration David became king over the twelve tribes.

11.0.9.en: The appointment of David as king was accomplished on the basis of the following: 1. His relationship with them, for they said to him: “Behold, we are thy bone and thy flesh” [1]. They boasted of their attachment to him. They came to him because they were of his bone and his flesh. But the Son of David came down to us, and made us of His flesh and His bones. The Apostle says: “For we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones” (Eph 5:30). The Lord Christ gave Himself as an example, for in His union with the Church, the Bride, as St. Augustine says, He left the Father, in that He emptied Himself of the glories and took the form of a servant (Phil 2:7), though He remained one with Him in essence without separation. He also left His mother, that is the Jewish people from whom He took the body through St. Mary, Jewish by race, that He might become one flesh with His Bride [1]. 2. Because of his conduct, especially that he did not stretch out his hand against Saul, who spared no effort to be rid of him. His love for his opponents drew them to him. St. Augustine says in his address to those preparing for the sacrament of Baptism: [Love alone is the distinguishing mark between the children of God and the children of the devil. Let us mark ourselves with the sign of the cross of Jesus Christ... and let us all be baptized. And let all come to the Church that we may build the walls of the Church, for there is nothing that distinguishes the children of God from the children of the devil except love.] 3. This was not accomplished by human strength, but according to the word of the Lord by Samuel. Samuel had earlier anointed him king at the command of the Lord (1 Sam 16:13), and now he was anointed a second time.

11.1.0.en: And moreover in time past, even when Saul was king, thou wast he that leddest out and broughtest in Israel: and the LORD thy God said unto thee,

11.1.1.en: Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be ruler over my people Israel.” [2]

11.1.2.en: The command was issued by the Lord Himself: the LORD thy God said unto thee that thou shalt feed my people Israel [2].

11.1.3.en: David, as king, occupied their hearts before he received the throne, even when Saul was king [2]. It was not the seat that made David king, but God made him king while he was a boy, before he sat on the throne!

11.1.4.en: What is recorded in this book in general, and in this chapter in particular, completes what is said of David the king in the books of Samuel and Kings. Perhaps David stood out in those books as a man of faith, with strength of personality, courage and works that were exceptional through the Lord. But what this book presents is that David is a godly man who loves the worship of the living temple.

11.1.5.en: In the earlier books we see David the saint and the sinner, yet faithful in consecrating his heart and all his depths to God.

11.1.6.en: In reality the two portraits of David’s character in the earlier books and in this book are not contradictory, but are one complete portrait.

11.1.7.en: The book does not refer here to the short and failed reign of Ishbosheth (2 Sam 2-4), but passes directly to the crowning of David as king.

11.1.8.en: The Second Book of Samuel has already given us many details concerning David’s attainment of power, where God uses the efforts of many people, some of them from Saul’s family; but what is affirmed here is that God is the One who directs events, accomplishing everything as He wills.

11.1.9.en: Saul tried to destroy or hinder the plan for David’s receiving power, but God is the Controller of history and the One who cares for His people, and He seated David as king at the appropriate time.

11.2.0.en: Therefore came all the elders of Israel to the king to Hebron; and David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the LORD; and they anointed David king over Israel, according to the word of the LORD by Samuel. [3]

11.2.1.en: All the elders of Israel gathered to King David in Hebron, and he made a covenant with them before the Lord.

11.2.2.en: Here he affirms that David’s ascent to the throne was not by chance, nor the fruit of David’s nobility and ability, but according to God’s plan and grace, and it is bound up with a divine promise declared to David while he was still a boy tending his father’s sheep.

11.2.3.en: David reigned over Judah seven and a half years before he reigned over all Israel and took Jerusalem, and twenty years after Samuel anointed him king (1 Sam 16:1-13). For everything with God has its appointed time.

11.2.4.en: The divine promise was fulfilled despite the difficulties that David faced, until the promise seemed impossible. Perhaps some thought that the mercies of God had forsaken him, but at the appropriate time they appeared. David’s troubles were by God’s permission, that he might truly experience God’s love, care and wisdom.

11.3.s.en: 2. The need for Jerusalem as a capital

11.3.0.en: 4 And David and all Israel went to Jerusalem, which is Jebus; where the Jebusites were, the inhabitants of the land. 5 And the inhabitants of Jebus said to David, “Thou shalt not come hither.” Nevertheless David took the castle of Zion, which is the city of David. 6 And David said, “Whosoever smiteth the Jebusites first shall be chief and captain.” So Joab the son of Zeruiah went first up, and was chief. 7 And David dwelt in the castle; therefore they called it the city of David. 8 And he built the city round about, even from Millo round about: and Joab repaired the rest of the city. 9 So David waxed greater and greater: for the LORD of hosts was with him.

11.3.1.en: Since all the tribes together enjoyed David as king, the need became pressing for a capital worthy of this nation.

11.3.2.en: The capture of Jerusalem and its establishment as the capital was a wise move by David and his men. For Jerusalem is close to the border between the southern tribes and the northern tribes, and it is considered an effective factor in uniting the tribes together, without arousing feelings of envy and jealousy among them. It can rightly be said that Jerusalem was the heart and center of the people, and it was the fitting place to set up a temple for the Lord, representing the divine presence in the midst of all the people [2].

11.3.3.en: Its population in the days of David’s reign was about two thousand; the number rose to five thousand in the days of Solomon, and to seven thousand before the captivity, and most likely fell to less than five thousand in the days when the book was written. And before the destruction of the second temple in A.D. 70 the number was more than 80 thousand [3]. Through the vicissitudes of history, this city that David established as a capital has remained the heart of Judea.

11.3.4.en: And David and all Israel went to Jerusalem (which is Jebus).

11.3.5.en: And the Jebusites were there, the inhabitants of the land. [4]

11.3.6.en: Much is said about Jerusalem in the Holy Bible, and the holy city took its name from the Salem of Melchizedek, and from the name of Mount Moriah where Abraham offered his son Isaac, for “Jehovah-jireh” is the name that Abraham gave to Mount Moriah (Gen 22:14), and the temple was built in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah.

11.4.0.en: The following verses speak of David’s building around Jerusalem; he took the castle of Zion, which had been in the hands of the Jebusites until then, and called it the city of David [7], and verse (6) of Psalm (2) (Ps 2:6) refers to this: “As for me, I have anointed my king on Zion, my holy mountain”; for the city of David is in reality the region of Mount Zion.

11.4.1.en: David chose Jerusalem as the capital of the kingdom for political and military reasons. Because it lay to a large extent between the borders of the tribes, near the center of the kingdom, its location was neutral, reducing the tribes’ jealousy of one another. It was also on a high mountain, which made attacking it difficult.

11.4.2.en: The Jebusites did not expect that any force could storm them, because of the impregnable walls of Jerusalem and its being surrounded by strong rocks. They reckoned that they were safe, and did not realize that God is the Rock who preserves His children, and the refuge of those who trust in Him.

11.4.3.en: David and all the men of Israel set out from Hebron to Jerusalem, which was called Jebus, and the Jebusites were dwelling there, and they refused the entry of David and his men. And just as David and his men dwelt in Jebus, which became “Jerusalem,” that is, the city of peace, so we dwell with the Son of David and the place is transformed into a new Jerusalem. St. Gregory of Nazianzus sees that Jerusalem is our new inheritance.

11.4.4.en: v Farewell, for our massive and renewed temple has become our inheritance, and the secret of its greatness is the Word (Jesus Christ); for it was once called “Jebus,” and now we have made it Jerusalem [4].

11.4.5.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus Jerusalem has become a symbol of heaven, as of the heart of the believer as the second heaven, for it is said:

11.4.6.en: “Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name” (Rev 3:12)

11.4.7.en: “I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev 21:2)

11.4.8.en: “And he carried me away in the spirit to a great and high mountain, and shewed me that great city, the holy Jerusalem, descending out of heaven from God” (Rev 21:10)

11.4.9.en: v Some define a city as a gathering of beings in one organized body, governed by law... This definition given to the city suits the Jerusalem above... the heavenly city, because there is the church of the firstborn, whose names are written in the heavens (Heb 12:23). For it is also organized, since the flow of the life of the saints never ceases and it is governed by the heavenly law. Human nature cannot comprehend the extent of the readiness and order of this city, for [Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him] (1 Cor 2:9). Also in this city there are myriads of angels... and the church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven (Heb 12:22-23)... David mentions this city and says: Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God (Ps 87:3). What God promised to this city Isaiah conveys to us: [I will make thee an eternal excellency.. a joy... of many generations] Violence shall no more be heard in thy land, wasting nor destruction within thy borders; but thou shalt call thy walls Salvation (Isa 60:15-18). Let us lift up the eyes of our souls, and let us seek the higher good things that befit the city of God [5].

11.4.10.en: v Sheep are earthly and bowed down to the earth, but man is a heavenly being, who rises above them both by the structure of his body and by the dignity of his spirit. What is the form of the animals that go on four feet? Their head is bowed down to the earth, and they look at their belly, and only follow the needs of their belly. But your head, O man, is raised toward heaven, and your eyes look upward; yet you descend through the passions of the flesh, and become a slave to your belly and its lusts. So you reach the level of the animals for no reason, and become like them. You are called to things more noble: “Seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God” (Col 3:1). Lift yourself above the world... make your conversation in heaven. For your true homeland is the heavenly Jerusalem, and your countrymen are “the church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven (Heb 12:23) [6].

11.5.0.en: And the inhabitants of Jebus said to David,

11.5.2.en: Nevertheless David took the castle of Zion (which is the city of David). [5]

11.5.3.en: It tells us of David’s capture of Jebus, or Jerusalem, and that it was called the city of David [4-9].

11.5.4.en: St. Jerome presents to us a spiritual meaning of the castle of Zion, or the fortress of Zion, in which we take refuge against those who come against us.

11.6.0.en: v You have great shrewdness and an inexhaustible store of language; your style is smooth and pure, and your eloquence and purity are mingled with wisdom. Your head is good and all your senses are kindled with intelligence. Add to this wisdom and eloquence earnest study and knowledge of the Holy Scripture. Then I shall soon see you in your fortress against all who come against you. You will go up with Joab on the roof of Zion and sing on the housetops what you have learned in the secret chambers [7].

11.7.0.en: And David said, “Whosoever smiteth the Jebusites first shall be chief and captain.”

11.7.1.en: So Joab the son of Zeruiah went first up, and was chief. [6]

11.7.2.en: Here alone among the other books it makes clear how Joab became the commander of David’s army [6-7], and it declared that Joab built the city and repaired it [8].

11.7.3.en: Joab, of whom the Book of Samuel does not speak, occupies the first place after David. We do not see him here as the ambitious and spiteful man, but as the one appointed according to God’s plan to overcome the castle of Zion for David the king. It is said of him that he smote the Jebusites and so became chief, and that he repaired a part of the city.

11.7.4.en: This book does not refer to Joab’s conflict with Abner and his revenge on this noble commander, just as it is silent about David’s sorrowful words: “And I am this day weak, though anointed king; and these men the sons of Zeruiah be too hard for me: the LORD shall reward the doer of evil according to his wickedness” (2 Sam 3:39).

11.8.0.en: This book did not criticize Joab but revealed everything positive in the life of Joab, and did not refer to David’s curse upon him (1 Kgs 2:5), and ignores what is negative in his life. What the book affirms is that God’s plan concerning David is being fulfilled, and that Joab and others are instruments for that [10].

11.9.0.en: And David dwelt in the castle; therefore they called it the city of David. [7]

11.10.0.en: And he built the city round about, even from Millo round about:

11.10.1.en: and Joab repaired the rest of the city. [8]

11.10.2.en: The writer ascribes to David the building of the walls, and to Joab the building of the houses, which is a work of little importance compared with the walls.

11.11.0.en: So David waxed greater and greater: for the LORD of hosts was with him [9]

11.11.1.en: The secret of David’s strength is the Lord, for it is said of him: “So David waxed greater and greater: for the LORD of hosts was with him” [9].

11.11.2.en: Saul used his strength and abilities for the sake of himself, his lust, his popularity and his authority, and so he collapsed; while David sought to enjoy the divine presence, so his stature increased, for the Almighty was with him. The secret of David’s success was his reliance on God, and the secret of Saul’s decline was his self-regard, ignoring God (1 Sam 15:17-26). What occupied David was the glory of God and his attachment to Him; therefore God lifted him from glory to glory.

11.11.3.en: St. Augustine sees in this expression the harmony between the free will that God gives to man and the divine work in the life of His believers, to give them the will, the word and the work. Thus we do not ignore David’s role in his success, but it is not accomplished without the grace of God, which gave him a holy will and the ability to work according to God’s will.

11.11.4.en: v Without doubt human wills cannot resist the will of God, who does whatever pleases Him in heaven and on earth (Isa 45:11).

11.11.5.en: The human will cannot prevent Him from doing what He wills, seeing that even by human wills He does what He wills, when He wills to do this...

11.11.6.en: Such was the case of David, whom God established over the kingdom with a joyful result.

11.11.7.en: We read of him: “So David waxed greater and greater: for the LORD of hosts was with him” [9]. A little later it is said: “Then the spirit came upon Amasai, who was chief of the thirty (the captains), and he said, Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse: peace, peace be unto thee, and peace be to thine helpers; for thy God helpeth thee” (1 Chr 12:18).

11.11.8.en: Could Amasai have opposed the will of God, even though he was fulfilling His will, seeing that God, through His Spirit with whom Amasai was clothed, worked in his heart that he should will thus, speak thus, and act thus?

11.11.9.en: In the same way, a little after that, the Scripture says: [All these men of war, that could keep rank, came with a perfect heart to Hebron, to make David king over all Israel] (1 Chr 12:38).

11.11.10.en: It is clear that by their own will they made David king; this fact is plain and cannot be denied. And yet it is God who works in human hearts as He wills, who wills and works this will in them. This is the reason for which the Scripture said first: “So David waxed greater and greater: for the LORD of hosts was with him” [9].

11.11.11.en: The Lord God who was with David brought these men to make him king. How did He make them so? Certainly not by binding them with any material chains. Rather He worked in them and took hold of their hearts, and drew them by their own will which He created in them. Therefore when God wills to set up kings on the earth, He takes hold of the wills of the multitude by His power, more than by human power itself.

11.11.12.en: If this is so, certainly it is He, and not another, who gives useful counsels and makes adjustments in the heart of the one to whom He gives counsel, so that he may dwell in the heavenly kingdom [8].

11.11.13.en: St. Augustine again affirms that God does not compel a man to do the will of God by force, but when a man surrenders his life into the hand of God, God works that this man should will and act according to the will of God [9].

11.11.14.en: This chapter highlights the greatness of the character of David and of the heroes attached to him: 1. David a leader from the Lord: God chose David for the purity of his heart and his faithfulness in little, that is, in tending his father’s sheep. Now all the men of Israel choose him, because they perceived how the Lord was with him, whereas Saul, though he was made king, was not faithful to the Lord. 2. David supports Joab to be a leader: David had his role in supporting Joab and in his taking up the leadership work. David was a capable leader, but he could not accomplish everything by himself. The successful leader raises up successful and faithful leaders who work with him. 3. Heroes glorified in a simple deed: Joab did a great deed, in that he smote the Jebusites [6]. But these three did not disdain to perform a simple deed, in bringing water from the well of Beth-lehem, that was at the gate [18]. Often the greatness of some shows in the practice of small things. 4. The great fall in matters in which the weak may not fall, such as David’s killing of Uriah the Hittite [41] in order to take his wife.

11.12.s.en: 3. A leader who raises up leaders

11.12.0.en: 10 These also are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel. 11 And this is the number of the mighty men whom David had; Jashobeam, an Hachmonite, the chief of the captains: he lifted up his spear against three hundred slain by him at one time. 12 And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite, who was one of the three mighties. 13 He was with David at Pasdammim, and there the Philistines were gathered together to battle, where was a parcel of ground full of barley; and the people fled from before the Philistines. 14 And they set themselves in the midst of that parcel, and delivered it, and slew the Philistines; and the LORD saved them by a great deliverance. 15 Now three of the thirty captains went down to the rock to David, into the cave of Adullam; and the host of the Philistines encamped in the valley of Rephaim. 16 And David was then in the hold, and the Philistines’ garrison was then at Beth-lehem. 17 And David longed, and said, “Oh that one would give me drink of the water of the well of Beth-lehem, that is at the gate!” 18 And the three brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Beth-lehem, that was by the gate, and took it, and brought it to David: but David would not drink of it, but poured it out to the LORD, 19 And said, “My God forbid it me, that I should do this thing: shall I drink the blood of these men that have put their lives in jeopardy? for with the jeopardy of their lives they brought it.” Therefore he would not drink it. These things did these three mightiest. 20 And Abishai the brother of Joab, he was chief of the three: for lifting up his spear against three hundred, he slew them, and had a name among the three. 21 Of the three, he was more honourable than the two; for he was their captain: howbeit he attained not to the first three. 22 Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done many acts; he slew two lionlike men of Moab: also he went down and slew a lion in a pit in a snowy day. 23 And he slew an Egyptian, a man of great stature, five cubits high; and in the Egyptian’s hand was a spear like a weaver’s beam; and he went down to him with a staff, and plucked the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand, and slew him with his own spear. 24 These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and had the name among the three mighties. 25 Behold, he was honourable among the thirty, but attained not to the first three: and David made him one of his confidants. 26 Also the valiant men of the armies were, Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Beth-lehem, 27 Shammoth the Harorite, Helez the Pelonite, 28 Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Abiezer the Antothite, 29 Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite, 30 Maharai the Netophathite, Heled the son of Baanah the Netophathite, 31 Ithai the son of Ribai of Gibeah, that pertained to the children of Benjamin, Benaiah the Pirathonite, 32 Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite, 33 Azmaveth the Baharumite, Eliahba the Shaalbonite, 34 The sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan the son of Shage the Hararite, 35 Ahiam the son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur, 36 Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite, 37 Hezro the Carmelite, Naarai the son of Ezbai, 38 Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar the son of Haggeri, 39 Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Berothite, the armourbearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah, 40 Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite, 41 Uriah the Hittite, Zabad the son of Ahlai, 42 Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a captain of the Reubenites, and thirty with him, 43 Hanan the son of Maachah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite, 44 Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jeiel the sons of Hothan the Aroerite, 45 Jediael the son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite, 46 Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite, 47 Eliel, and Obed, and Jasiel the Mesobaite.

11.12.1.en: The successful leader supports many, that they may become leaders: 1. Joab the head: he said: [Whosoever smiteth the Jebusites first shall be chief and captain] [6]. Joab succeeded as chief of David’s warriors. 2. Three leaders [11-19]: David longed to drink water from the well of Beth-lehem that was at the gate [17]. What is this well but the work of the Holy Spirit in the Incarnation of the Word in Beth-lehem, which opened the gates of heaven? David did not drink the water, but offered it as a libation to the Lord; what he asks of leaders is for the sake of the Lord [18]. 3. Three other leaders, headed by Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, who slew two lionlike men of Moab and a lion in a pit in a snowy day [22], and killed the Egyptian giant with a staff [23]. The lion signifies the devil (1 Pet 5:8), and the Egyptian giant the love of the world. 4. The valiant men of the armies [26-47]: some of them were by birth enemies of Israel, from nations that opposed Israel, who became servants for the sake of the Kingdom of God. Among these: Zelek the Ammonite [39], Ithmah the Moabite [46], and Uriah the Hittite [41].

11.13.0.en: It is clear that David’s character, with its godliness together with its courage and sincerity, drew many men of valor and military leaders to work with him. 1. This chapter presents to us Joab as chief of David’s warriors. 2. The chapter referred to a group called the “three” [11] who seem to have had a special standing as heroes. 3. After them came the group of “the thirty,” who are the most prominent figures among David’s warriors in his early days, previously mentioned in (2 Sam 23:24-39); most of them from the house of David and some from the other tribes. 4. The number increased with those coming from the other tribes as a result of his growing popularity, so the book added 16 persons to the list of the thirty, perhaps to confirm the growth of David’s popularity.

11.13.1.en: The list of the army chiefs was set down at the beginning of his reign. In (2 Sam 23) we find a similar list set down at the end of his reign. A few names that appear in Samuel do not appear here, but a large number has been added. The chapter refers to 81 mighty men, 20 of whom are mentioned without their names being given, while in Samuel (chapter 23) 37 of them are mentioned. In Second Samuel the mighty men are mentioned as supporters of David in establishing his throne. But here it is to recognize God’s plan and His work in establishing the throne for His anointed.

11.13.2.en: These mighty men came to David at different times. Some came when he was in the cave of Adullam [15-19], some when he was in Ziklag (1 Chr 12:1-22), and others when he was in Hebron (1 Chr 12:23-40).

11.13.3.en: These also are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel. [10]

11.13.4.en: Divine inspiration affirmed that the secret of the increase of David’s greatness is that the LORD of hosts was with him [9], and immediately it began to speak of the chief of the mighty men whom he had.

11.13.5.en: When the believer is in fellowship with the LORD of hosts, his success is not confined to his own personal growth, but extends also to those who work with him. It is not fitting for the great to ascribe their greatness to themselves in arrogance and pride, but to God who works in them and in those who work with them.

11.13.6.en: God works through us and in us by His grace, which also works in those who work with us! The sign of being with God is that He works through all; for God is all in all, and wills to work through everyone.

11.13.7.en: David strengthened himself with God, the God of hosts, and those who worked with him strengthened themselves with him, and all Israel strengthened themselves with them [10].

11.13.8.en: The work of God in the life of His people is that the faithful leader urges him to raise up leaders who grow in everything, and the leaders work on behalf of the whole community, and the community as a whole supports the king or the president or the leader. A wonderful fellowship between God and man, and between man and his fellow man.

11.13.9.en: The chief mighty men whom David had were those who followed him in the period of his rejection, and now that he has been raised to the throne, these also were raised, and here we find something necessary for our benefit.

11.13.10.en: David was a type of our Lord Jesus, who calls His believers His people, and they are [the mighty men whom He has]. At His coming the Lord Jesus was rejected by many. His own said: [We will not have this man to reign over us]. In these days of ours Christ is rejected by the world, so we are living in the period of the rejection of Christ, and He is calling His mighty men.

11.13.11.en: The following is a list of some of David’s men, mighty men of valor, and a few of their great deeds:

11.14.0.en: And this is the number of the mighty men whom David had;

11.14.1.en: Jashobeam, an Hachmonite, the chief of the captains:

11.14.2.en: he lifted up his spear against three hundred slain by him at one time. [11]

11.14.3.en: With his spear he killed three hundred at one time. God gave him a victory beyond nature over the enemies of his people.

11.15.s.en: B. Eleazar the son of Dodo

11.15.0.en: 12 And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite, who was one of the three mighties. 13 He was with David at Pasdammim, and there the Philistines were gathered together to battle, where was a parcel of ground full of barley; and the people fled from before the Philistines. 14 And they set themselves in the midst of that parcel, and delivered it, and slew the Philistines; and the LORD saved them by a great deliverance.

11.15.1.en: And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite,

11.15.2.en: who was one of the three mighties. [12]

11.15.3.en: Eleazar the son of Dodo the Ahohite was faithful to David; he accompanied him even when the others forsook him.

11.16.0.en: He was with David at Pasdammim, and there the Philistines were gathered together to battle,

11.16.1.en: where was a parcel of ground full of barley; and the people fled from before the Philistines. [13]

11.16.2.en: All who were around David fled before the Philistines, but Eleazar stood firm in his place, therefore the Lord saved him. The most dangerous enemy of man is fear; but whoever stands firm with courage, trusting in God, enjoys victory.

11.17.0.en: And they set themselves in the midst of that parcel, and delivered it, and slew the Philistines;

11.17.1.en: and the LORD saved them by a great deliverance. [14]

11.17.2.en: All who were around Eleazar the son of Dodo fled before the Philistines, and he stood firm in his place, so the Lord saved him. He was a symbolic image of the Lord Christ in the midst of His sufferings, when He said: “Behold, the hour cometh, yea, is now come, that ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (Jn 16:32).

11.17.3.en: When everyone forsakes a man, and he stands firm in God and does not waver, he enjoys victory.

11.17.4.en: If David and the heroes and all the people magnify themselves in God, the LORD of hosts, then all ought to strive not against men but against the powers of darkness (Eph 6:12), for the pagan Philistines signify evil and the powers of darkness. It is fitting for us to fight the good fight (2 Tim 4:7).

11.18.0.en: 15 Now three of the thirty captains went down to the rock to David, into the cave of Adullam; and the host of the Philistines encamped in the valley of Rephaim. 16 And David was then in the hold, and the Philistines’ garrison was then at Beth-lehem. 17 And David longed, and said, “Oh that one would give me drink of the water of the well of Beth-lehem, that is at the gate!” 18 And the three brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Beth-lehem, that was by the gate, and took it, and brought it to David: but David would not drink of it, but poured it out to the LORD, 19 And said, “My God forbid it me, that I should do this thing: shall I drink the blood of these men that have put their lives in jeopardy? for with the jeopardy of their lives they brought it.” Therefore he would not drink it. These things did these three mightiest.

11.18.1.en: Now three of the thirty captains went down to the rock to David, into the cave of Adullam; and the host of the Philistines encamped in the valley of Rephaim. [15]

11.18.2.en: The story of the three heroes was preserved by the Book of Chronicles to reveal what was in David’s heart toward God and his intense concern for the life of his followers.

11.18.3.en: These thirty were the bravest and greatest leaders in David’s army. The three men who were set apart as the dearest of the heroes are those who brought David water from the well of Beth-lehem. This story carries a great symbolism, for David was brought up in Beth-lehem as his birthplace. And there was a well at its entrance; he would often return thirsty after tending the sheep and then drink from that well. And now he was besieged by the Philistines and could not go to that well, so he said: “Oh that one would give me drink of the water of the well of Beth-lehem, that is at the gate!” It was merely a wish and was not a command, but the three brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Beth-lehem, that was by the gate, and took it, and brought it to David. And the astonishing thing is that he would not drink it but poured it out as an offering to the LORD.

11.18.4.en: Here are similarities on which we can meditate. The Lord Jesus was born in Beth-lehem and He is this water from Beth-lehem; He is the water of life, and there are many mighty men through the generations and centuries who belong to Jesus Christ, who have brought this water to the thirsty world. And we notice that David’s men responded to the mere expression of a wish by him. For he could not give a command like this. And here is our Lord Jesus commanding us to take the water of life to the whole world; so what have we done with it? Are we obedient to His commands?

11.18.5.en: We also notice what David did with this water that was brought to him at great risk. David was not selfish, and it is no wonder that his men loved him and were ready to suffer for him, because he was ready to suffer with them. He did not drink the water, because his men had no water, and he preferred to be like them. The Psalm (1 Chr 22:14) tells us that at the death of our Lord Jesus Christ on the cross He said: “I am poured out like water”; He poured out His life like water on the earth, and took His place among us as one of us — taking what is ours to give us what is His — taking our body and giving us His Holy Spirit, and making us one with Him by His goodness [10].

11.19.0.en: And David was then in the hold, and the Philistines’ garrison was then at Beth-lehem. [16]

11.20.1.en: “Oh that one would give me drink of the water of the well of Beth-lehem, that is at the gate!” [17]

11.20.2.en: The water that David asked for from Beth-lehem signifies the Lord Christ, who was born in Beth-lehem.

11.20.3.en: v By the water that David the king desired, what did he long for, but the Son, who is the water of life for him who seeks Him?

11.20.4.en: Christ was called by the name of water, because he thirsted for Him, and it was known that He would come to the earth from Beth-lehem.

11.20.5.en: That seer (David) did not ask for water that issues from a spring, because the Son of God is not from marriage.

11.20.6.en: The water of the cistern comes from the top of the height, as Christ came down from on high, to become a drink.

11.20.7.en: The cistern is the Virgin, because the drink came down into her from on high, and no fountain rose up from the earth and poured the water into her.

11.20.8.en: The woman is also called a cistern in prophecy, and the man a mountain, and let him who reads understand [11].

11.20.9.en: St. Jacob of Serugh St. Augustine sees in the pouring out of the water as an offering a reference to the concept of fasting, that it is not a restraint or a shattering of the old passions, but replacing them with new and fitting joys.

11.20.10.en: v Keeping the Great Fast is not a restraint of the old passions, but an opportunity for new joys. Take into account, offering it with every possible diligence, that you prevent these situations from creeping up on you. The filling of the stomach must be blamed. Therefore the incentives to lust must be removed. For fasting is not a loathing of certain kinds of food, but a control of the fleshly lust... So the holy king David repented because of his excessive desire for water [12].

11.21.0.en: And the three brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Beth-lehem, that was by the gate, and took it, and brought it to David: but David would not drink of it, but poured it out to the LORD [18]

11.21.1.en: They risked their lives to bring water to David from the well of Beth-lehem. They did not do this to receive a word of praise, nor were their names mentioned. What concerned them was the joy of David’s heart.

11.21.2.en: It is fitting for us, when someone wishes to serve us or give us something for the sake of God who works in us, to offer this service or gift to God in the life of the needy. For what God gives us through them is a trust that we also offer to others, and He reckons it a gift offered to Himself personally.

11.21.3.en: He refused to drink the water, perhaps because he felt remorse that he had expressed his wish to drink from the well of Beth-lehem, since it was fitting for him to care for those around him, for they might have been more in need of water than he.

11.22.0.en: And said, “My God forbid it me, that I should do this thing:

11.22.1.en: shall I drink the blood of these men that have put their lives in jeopardy?

11.22.2.en: for with the jeopardy of their lives they brought it.”

11.22.3.en: Therefore he would not drink it.

11.22.4.en: These things did these three mightiest. [19]

11.22.5.en: These men risked their lives to please David, and they realized that their consecration to him came from their consecration to God, therefore he poured out the water as a drink offering, showing that God alone deserves such consecration. They offered the water to David, and he in turn offered it to God. For he reckoned that God alone deserves such consecration.

11.22.6.en: When we serve others for the sake of the Lord, we are serving God Himself.

11.22.7.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that those who share in the expenses of the preachers are reckoned as having contributed to the work of preaching.

11.23.s.en: D. Abishai the brother of Joab

11.23.0.en: And Abishai the brother of Joab, he was chief of the three:

11.23.1.en: for lifting up his spear against three hundred, he slew them, and had a name among the three. [20]

11.24.0.en: Of the three, he was more honourable than the two; for he was their captain: howbeit he attained not to the first three. [21]

11.24.1.en: Abshai (Abishai) the brother of Joab is considered the most honored of the three. The Holy Bible tells us that in his faithfulness to David he was steadfast without hesitation. He went with him to Saul’s camp (1 Sam 26), and accompanied him in his flight from Jerusalem when Absalom rebelled against him (2 Sam 16), and he it was who crushed the rebellion of Sheba (2 Sam 20), and delivered David from the giant Ishbi-benob (2 Sam 21). He rendered him services with all faithfulness (2 Sam 10; 18; 1 Chr 18).

11.24.2.en: Thus with courage, sincerity and self-sacrifice he served David; how much more is it fitting for us to serve the Lord of David, the King of kings?

11.25.s.en: E. Benaiah the son of Jehoiada

11.25.0.en: 22 Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done many acts; he slew two lionlike men of Moab: also he went down and slew a lion in a pit in a snowy day. 23 And he slew an Egyptian, a man of great stature, five cubits high; and in the Egyptian’s hand was a spear like a weaver’s beam; and he went down to him with a staff, and plucked the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand, and slew him with his own spear. 24 These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and had the name among the three mighties. 25 Behold, he was honourable among the thirty, but attained not to the first three: and David made him one of his confidants.

11.25.1.en: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done many acts;

11.25.2.en: he slew two lionlike men of Moab: also he went down and slew a lion in a pit in a snowy day. [22]

11.25.3.en: The secret of the strength of these heroes is that the Lord who was with David was also with them. Joshua’s advice came: [Cleave unto the LORD your God, as ye have done unto this day. For the LORD hath driven out from before you great nations and strong: but as for you, no man hath been able to stand before you unto this day. One man of you shall chase a thousand: for the LORD your God, he it is that fighteth for you, as he hath promised you] (Josh 23:8-11).

11.26.0.en: And he slew an Egyptian, a man of great stature, five cubits high; and in the Egyptian’s hand was a spear like a weaver’s beam;

11.26.1.en: and he went down to him with a staff, and plucked the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand, and slew him with his own spear. [23]

11.26.2.en: His father was a valiant priest (1 Chr 27:5).

11.26.3.en: He was chief over David’s guards. He took the place of Joab, the commander of the armies of Israel (1 Kgs 2:34-35). His victories present to us a picture of the life that is victorious over the world (Egypt), the flesh (Moab), and Satan (the prowling lion), for he overcame all these.

11.27.0.en: These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and had the name among the three mighties. [24]

11.27.1.en: Behold, he was honourable among the thirty, but attained not to the first three.

11.28.0.en: And David made him one of his confidants. [25]

11.28.1.en: Also the valiant men of the armies were, Asahel the brother of Joab,

11.29.0.en: Elhanan the son of Dodo of Beth-lehem, [26]

11.30.0.en: Shammoth the Harorite, Helez the Pelonite, [27]

11.31.0.en: Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Abiezer the Antothite, [28]
